---
title: "AADTBench: an open, extensible benchmark for estimating street-level flows of people and vehicles"
author:
  - name: Robin Lovelace
    affiliation: University of Leeds
  - name: Crispin Cooper
    affiliation: Cardiff University
date: today
bibliography: references.bib
abstract: |
  Many tools estimate how many people, cycles or vehicles use each street, from
  network centrality and spatial interaction models to traffic assignment. They
  are rarely compared on the same counts, network and inputs, so it is hard to
  know which to use. We present AADTBench version 0.2, an open benchmark and
  harness for this task. It fixes frozen cases (network, counts, a documented
  count-to-link crosswalk, input tiers and spatial splits) and scores any tool
  that writes one flow per link. Each result is scored twice: on raw flows and
  after one shared reference calibrator with road class, so tools are compared
  on the signal they add. Four simple baselines are mandatory. Methods are
  grouped into model families (reach, flow, assignment) so that like is
  compared with like. The first release has six cases in four cities with
  counts for walking, cycling, cars and heavy vehicles. We report two open
  tools, cityseer and AequilibraE, against the baselines. For motor traffic,
  road class explains most of what can be predicted and the tools add little.
  For walking and cycling, attractor and population density baselines beat
  routed flows on every open case. Porting AequilibraE to the adapter contract
  took one file and exposed friction that we fixed in the contract. Data are
  released as versioned, checksummed assets and every result carries a
  hardware record. We invite contributions of tools, cases and counts.
keywords: [traffic flow estimation, benchmark, spatial network analysis, active travel, traffic counts, reproducibility, open data]
execute:
  freeze: auto

```{python}
#| include: false
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import yaml
from IPython.display import Markdown

ROOT = Path("..")
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, str(ROOT))
from benchmark.fetch import fetch_result

# Results are release assets. A local run (results/) takes precedence.
board = pd.read_csv(fetch_result("leaderboard.csv", dest=ROOT / "results"))
board = board[board["status"] == "complete"]
OPEN = ["oxford-v1", "leeds-v2", "bristol-v1", "melbourne-v1", "leeds-v1"]
CASES = OPEN + ["leuven-v1"]
go = board[board["split"] == "group_out_pooled"]
cal = go[go["track"] == "calibrated"]
raw = go[go["track"] == "raw"]
ENGINES = [("cityseer_od", "default", "T2_synthetic_od", "cityseer"),
           ("aequilibrae", "aon", "T2_synthetic_od", "AequilibraE AoN"),
           ("aequilibrae", "ue_bfw", "T2_synthetic_od", "AequilibraE UE")]
BASELINES = ["class_only", "centre_distance", "attractor_density", "population_density"]


def pick(df, tool, variant, tier, col="q"):
    d = df[(df.tool == tool) & (df.variant == variant) & (df.input_tier == tier)]
    return d.set_index(["case_id", "mode"])[col]


def fmt(v, nd=2):
    return "" if pd.isna(v) else f"{v:.{nd}f}"
```

# Introduction

Planners need to know how many people walk, cycle or drive along each street.
Counts exist for a small share of links. Models fill the gaps. The methods are
many: network centrality and reach measures from spatial network analysis
[@cooper2020sdna; @simons2022cityseer; @sevtsuk2025madina], demand-weighted
betweenness and spatial interaction, and origin-destination (OD) assignment
with or without congestion [@aequilibrae2024; @krantz2024flownet]. Each is
usually validated on its own counts, network and inputs. So it is hard to say
which method to use, for which mode, and at what cost.

Benchmarks have solved this problem in other fields. A benchmark fixes the
task, the data and the scoring, and lets anyone submit a method. Version 0.1
of AADTBench did this for one case: two-way motor traffic on 49 held-out links
in Leeds. Three lessons from that version, and from a larger private
experiment in five cities, shaped version 0.2:

1. Raw modelled flow fits counts poorly. Calibration with road class does most
   of the work. A benchmark that only scores calibrated output cannot tell what
   a tool adds.
2. Simple baselines are strong. In the private experiments, attractor density
   beat routed cycling flow in every city.
3. Small held-out sets in one city are fragile, and counts close to each other
   are correlated, so random splits overstate skill
   [@roberts2017crossvalidation].

This paper describes the benchmark design (Section 2), the harness and how to
add a tool (Section 3), and the current performance of two open tools on the
available cases (Section 4). Section 5 discusses what the results mean and
what the benchmark cannot yet say. Section 6 invites contributions.

# Benchmark design

## Task and target

The target is the two-way annual average daily flow on a link, for one of five
modes: walking, cycling, car (motor vehicles other than heavy vehicles), heavy
(goods vehicles plus buses and coaches) and motor (all motor vehicles, for
cases whose counts do not separate them). A tool writes one non-negative flow
per link and mode. The flow can be on any scale.

## Cases

A case is a frozen bundle: a network with stable link ids, count sites with
annual averages, a crosswalk from sites to links, input layers, and spatial
folds. Cases are versioned. A change to any file makes a new version. Data are
distributed as assets of a GitHub release with a manifest of file sizes and
SHA-256 hashes, and the harness refuses files that do not match.
@tbl-cases lists the first release.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-cases
#| tbl-cap: "Cases in release v0.2.0. Sites are counted after the licence filter and the crosswalk (matched sites only). Leuven is all Telraam data (CC BY-NC 4.0) and is released as a separate non-commercial case."
rows = []
for c in CASES:
    y = yaml.safe_load((ROOT / "cases" / c / "case.yaml").read_text())
    n = go[go.case_id == c].drop_duplicates("mode").set_index("mode")["n_sites"]
    rows.append({"Case": c, "Place": y.get("place", y.get("title", "")),
                 "Licence class": y.get("licence_class", "open"),
                 **{m: (int(n[m]) if m in n else "") for m in ["walking", "cycling", "car", "heavy", "motor"]}})
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

The counts come from public sources with licences that allow redistribution:
the UK Open Government Licence (DfT, Oxfordshire County Council) and CC BY 4.0 (City of
Melbourne, Victoria Department of Transport and Planning). Sources with
non-commercial or per-authority terms are dropped from open cases. Networks and
points of interest come from OpenStreetMap [@haklay2008osm] and population from
WorldPop [@tatem2017worldpop]. A small central Oxford case (3 km radius) is
used for continuous integration.

## Count-to-link crosswalk

Placing counts on the wrong link causes large errors that look like model
error. So the crosswalk is built once by one open script with written rules: a
count can only match a link open to its mode, a road name or number is used
when present, motor counts prefer the most important road class among close
candidates, dual carriageways are paired so that two-way counts meet two-way
predictions, and turning counts and segment counts have their own rules. As a
check, the crosswalk agrees with an independent placement on 95 to 96 percent
of sites in the three UK cities. In Melbourne the agreement is lower (44
percent), mostly because counts sit on nodes shared by adjacent links of the
same road, where either choice gives a similar flow.

## Input tiers

Each run declares how much information it used. `T0` is the network only.
`T1` adds population and point-of-interest layers. `T2` adds a synthetic
gravity OD table per mode, built by the benchmark from those layers. `T3` adds
observed OD, which only the Leeds legacy case has (2011 census journeys to
work [@lovelace2017pct]). Results are compared within a tier first.

## Model families

Centrality, betweenness and gravity models overlap. Betweenness is a flow
model. Gravity is a form of reach with a continuous distance decay in place of
a step at a radius. So the benchmark groups methods into families rather than
tools: reach (closeness, gravity, sDNA's network quantity penalised by
distance), flow (betweenness, demand-weighted betweenness, spatial
interaction), and assignment (OD assignment with route choice or congestion).
Each run declares its options: distance metric (metric, angular or time),
radius or decay, weighting (none, population, land use or OD) and congestion.
The leaderboard groups rows by family. A reach score is not ranked against a
flow score without saying so.

## Tracks, baselines and splits

Every run is scored on two tracks. The *raw* track multiplies the submitted
flow by one scale factor, the geometric mean ratio of counts to flows on the
training folds. The *calibrated* track passes the flow through one shared
reference calibrator, fitted on the training folds:

$$\log(c + 1) = a + b \log(f + 1) + \gamma_{\text{class}} + \varepsilon,$$

where $c$ is the count, $f$ the flow and $\gamma$ a road class effect.
Predictions are back-transformed with Duan's smearing factor
[@duan1983smearing]. The calibrator is the same for every tool, so the
calibrated track asks what signal a tool adds beyond road class.

Four baselines are scored on every case and mode through the same calibrator:
road class only, distance from the centre, point-of-interest weight within
500 m, and population within 1 km. A tool that does not beat them adds little.

Sites are grouped into 3 km grid cells and the cells are split into five
folds. Each fold is predicted by a calibrator fitted on the other four, and
the pooled out-of-fold predictions are scored once. A second board fits the
calibrator on all other cities and scores the held-out city
(leave-one-city-out). No per-city tuning is allowed.

## Metrics

Each target reports the Spearman rank correlation ($\rho$), predictive $R^2$
on $\log(1 + \text{count})$, $R^2$ on the natural scale, and the calibration
ratio (sum of counts over sum of unscaled flow). The ranking summary is
$q = (\rho + R^2_{\log}) / 2$. Targets with fewer than 20 sites are shown but
not ranked.

# The harness

## Adapter contract

A tool joins the benchmark through an adapter: one Python file that
subclasses `Adapter`, declares its family, options, tiers, modes and fixed
variants, and implements `predict`. The harness gives the adapter a blind copy
of the case, with the network and the inputs its tier allows, and no counts.
The adapter returns a table of `segment_id`, `mode` and `flow`. The harness
writes the predictions, a run record and a hardware record, then does all
matching, calibration and scoring. Each tool can ship its own container image,
so its dependencies do not leak into the harness.

## Fast loops and provenance

`run_all` runs any set of tools on any set of cases, reuses cached runs whose
input hash has not changed, scores both tracks and both splits, rebuilds the
leaderboard, and appends every scored row to a results log with the git commit
and a time stamp. Every run writes a `system.json` with the CPU model, cores,
threads, RAM, operating system, kernel, container image digest, tool version,
harness commit, data release, wall time, CPU time and peak memory. The
leaderboard accepts only runs with this record. Because seconds depend on the
machine, each machine also times a fixed reference workload, and each run
reports a speed index: its wall time over the reference time.

Continuous integration runs the unit tests, the contract check and the scorer
on every pull request, plus a smoke test for each open tool in its own
container on the Oxford mini case. The smoke test checks that predictions are
valid and pass sanity bounds, for example that the calibrated track beats the
class-only baseline.

## Adding a tool: AequilibraE as the test

To test the contract we ported AequilibraE [@aequilibrae2024], a traffic
assignment package, from the v0.1 code. The port is one file with two fixed
variants, all-or-nothing (AoN) and user equilibrium with the bi-conjugate
Frank-Wolfe algorithm and BPR delay. As a check, AoN vehicle-metres on Oxford
car trips match an independent shortest path computation within 0.2 percent.
The port exposed friction in the contract, which we fixed there rather than in
the adapter: one unsupported mode used to sink a whole run (now recorded per
mode), assignment tools need a shared capacity table and a peak-hour factor
for daily OD (now in the contract), and all-motor OD was undefined where a
case splits car and heavy (now the sum). Remaining friction, such as compact
node ids and progress bars on standard error, is documented.

# Results

## Calibrated track

@tbl-main shows the calibrated track for the open cases. The best baseline is
shown next to each tool.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-main
#| tbl-cap: "Calibrated track, spatial group-out (five folds of 3 km cells). Values are q = (rho + log R2) / 2. Best baseline is the highest of the four mandatory baselines (T1). Tools use the T2 synthetic OD."
bl = cal[cal.tool == "baseline"]
best = bl.loc[bl.groupby(["case_id", "mode"])["q"].idxmax()].set_index(["case_id", "mode"])
rows = []
for (c, m), r in best.iterrows():
    if c not in OPEN:
        continue
    row = {"Case": c, "Mode": m, "Sites": int(r["n_sites"]),
           "Class only": fmt(pick(bl, "baseline", "class_only", "T1_open_covariates").get((c, m))),
           "Best baseline": f"{fmt(r['q'])} ({r['variant'].replace('_', ' ')})"}
    for tool, var, tier, lab in ENGINES:
        row[lab] = fmt(pick(cal, tool, var, tier).get((c, m)))
    rows.append(row)
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-main
#| fig-cap: "Calibrated q by case and mode (spatial group-out). Each row is a target. Higher is better. Points show the best baseline (circle), cityseer (square) and AequilibraE UE or AoN where UE is not defined (triangle). The same values are in Table 2."
#| fig-format: png

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

order = [(c, m) for c in OPEN for m in ["walking", "cycling", "car", "heavy", "motor"]
         if (c, m) in best.index]
labels = [f"{c} {m}" for c, m in order]
cs = pick(cal, "cityseer_od", "default", "T2_synthetic_od")
ue = pick(cal, "aequilibrae", "ue_bfw", "T2_synthetic_od")
aon = pick(cal, "aequilibrae", "aon", "T2_synthetic_od")
aeq = [ue.get(k, np.nan) if not pd.isna(ue.get(k, np.nan)) else aon.get(k, np.nan) for k in order]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.6))
y = np.arange(len(order))[::-1]
ax.axvline(0, color="#b8b8b2", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#ececea", lw=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.scatter([best.loc[k, "q"] for k in order], y, s=42, marker="o", color="#2a78d6", label="Best baseline", zorder=3, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1)
ax.scatter([cs.get(k, np.nan) for k in order], y, s=40, marker="s", color="#eb6834", label="cityseer", zorder=3, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1)
ax.scatter(aeq, y, s=48, marker="^", color="#1baf7a", label="AequilibraE", zorder=3, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1)
ax.set_yticks(y)
ax.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=8, color="#3d3d3a")
ax.set_xlabel("Calibrated q (higher is better)", fontsize=9, color="#3d3d3a")
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=8, colors="#3d3d3a")
for s in ["top", "right", "left"]:
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, frameon=False, loc="lower left")
fig.tight_layout()
```

For motor traffic (car, heavy and motor), road class does most of the work.
The class-only baseline scores q between 0.42 and 0.68 across the open cases,
and the best tool improves on it by at most about 0.03 (for example Oxford car
0.68 for cityseer against 0.67, and Bristol car 0.65 for both tools against
0.63). For heavy vehicles the tools are at most 0.01 above the best baseline,
and often below it.

For walking and cycling the picture is different. The density baselines are
the best predictors on every open case: point-of-interest density for walking
in Oxford (0.54) and Leeds (0.42), population density for walking in Melbourne
(0.29) and for cycling in Oxford (0.35), and distance from the centre for
cycling in Leeds (0.25). Both tools score lower, and often below zero, once
their flows go through the reference calibrator.

## Raw track

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-raw
#| tbl-cap: "Raw track, spatial group-out: Spearman rho between counts and scaled flows, and the share of sites where the tool gave zero flow. rho does not depend on the scale factor."
rows = []
for c in OPEN:
    for m in ["walking", "cycling", "car", "heavy", "motor"]:
        row = {"Case": c, "Mode": m}
        any_ = False
        for tool, var, tier, lab in ENGINES:
            v = pick(raw, tool, var, tier, "rho").get((c, m), np.nan)
            any_ = any_ or not pd.isna(v)
            row[f"{lab} rho"] = fmt(v)
        if any_:
            rows.append(row)
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

Ranked by raw flow alone, the tools carry real signal: Spearman $\rho$ is
0.47 to 0.66 for car, 0.38 to 0.54 for cycling with cityseer, and 0.26 to 0.38
for walking in Leeds and Oxford (@tbl-raw). For walking and cycling the raw
rank correlation is higher than the calibrated one (for example Oxford cycling
with cityseer: 0.49 raw, 0.22 calibrated). The reason is the spatial split.
Walking counts differ by an order of magnitude between folds (the median
Oxford walking count per fold ranges from about 100 to about 1,100), so road
class effects learned in some parts of a city transfer badly to others. The
raw $q$ is strongly negative because links where a tool gives zero flow
(between 9 and 18 percent of sites for cityseer in Oxford) are scored as zero.
We keep the penalty: a model that says nobody uses a counted street is wrong.

## Demand and congestion

The Leeds legacy case allows a direct test of observed against synthetic OD.
With census OD (`T3`), raw $\rho$ rises from 0.27 to 0.44 for cityseer and from
0.28 to 0.40 for AequilibraE UE. After calibration the gain almost vanishes
(q 0.53 against 0.52 for cityseer, 0.51 for both tiers with UE), because road
class already captures much of what better demand adds. User equilibrium
improves on AoN for car in Bristol (raw $\rho$ 0.59 against 0.55) and Leeds
(0.66 against 0.64), but changes little elsewhere.

## Leave one city out

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-loco
#| tbl-cap: "Leave-one-city-out, calibrated track: the calibrator is fitted on the other open cases for the same mode and scored on the held-out city. Values are q."
lo = board[(board.split == "leave_one_city_out") & (board.track == "calibrated")]
rows = []
for (c, m), g in lo.groupby(["case_id", "mode"]):
    b = g[g.tool == "baseline"]
    rb = b.loc[b["q"].idxmax()]
    row = {"Case": c, "Mode": m, "Best baseline": f"{fmt(rb['q'])} ({rb['variant'].replace('_', ' ')})"}
    for tool, var, tier, lab in ENGINES:
        row[lab] = fmt(pick(g, tool, var, tier).get((c, m)))
    rows.append(row)
Markdown(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_markdown(index=False, disable_numparse=True))
```

Moving the calibrator between cities costs skill for motor traffic in some
cities (Melbourne car falls from 0.59 to about 0.37, Oxford car from 0.68 to
0.51) and little in others (Leeds car stays at about 0.70). Point-of-interest
density remains the best walking predictor in every held-out city
(@tbl-loco). Cycling in Leeds is poorly predicted by any pooled calibrator,
which suggests that cycling levels differ between cities in ways the inputs do
not capture.

All runs finish in seconds to a minute on a desktop machine (@tbl-resources).
The hardware record of every run is in its `system.json`.

# Discussion

Three findings stand out. First, for motor traffic in these cities, the
signal a routing or betweenness model adds beyond road class is small. Road
class is itself the outcome of a century of planning for motor traffic, so it
already encodes much of the network position that the models compute. A
benchmark that only reported calibrated scores without a class-only baseline
would credit the models with skill they do not add.

Second, for walking and cycling, simple density measures beat the routed flows
we tested. This repeats, on open data and with a public harness, what we saw
in private experiments. It does not show that network models cannot predict
active travel. The tools were run with fixed, generic settings and a synthetic
gravity OD, and reach-family measures (gravity and closeness with
destinations, sDNA's NQPD) were not yet tested. These are the obvious next
submissions, and the family grouping exists so they can be compared fairly.

Third, the choice of evaluation changes the answer. Raw rank correlation,
calibrated skill, spatial group-out and leave-one-city-out each tell a
different part of the story. Reporting them side by side, with baselines, is
the main contribution of the benchmark.

## Limitations

The cases are four cities, three of them British. Counts are uneven across
modes: Bristol has no open walking counts and Melbourne no open cycling
counts. The UK cases use DfT short-period counts expanded to annual averages,
which are noisier than continuous counters. The networks are frozen
OpenStreetMap extracts cleaned before export, so their quality varies by city.
The synthetic OD is one simple gravity model. The reference calibrator is
log-linear with road class only. A mode-specific calibrator, for example
without class effects for walking, might be fairer to tools for active modes,
and is a candidate for a later version. Leuven is too small to rank and its
counts are seven-day means.

# Contributing

The benchmark is meant to grow. We invite three kinds of contribution:

- **Tools.** Write an adapter (one file, see `IMPLEMENTATIONS.md`), declare its
  family and options, and open a pull request. CI checks it on the mini case.
  sDNA, including its NQPD reach model, flownet, madina and space syntax tools
  are natural next adapters.
- **Cases.** Any city with open counts and a redistributable licence can
  become a case. Cities with continuous walking and cycling counters are the
  most valuable.
- **Rules.** The crosswalk rules, the calibrator and the splits are versioned.
  Proposals to change them go through issues and create a new benchmark
  version, so old results stay valid.

# Data and code availability

Code: <https://github.com/Robinlovelace/aadtbench>. Case data: release v0.2.0
of the same repository, with a manifest of SHA-256 hashes. Counts are under
the UK Open Government Licence v3 or CC BY 4.0, networks and points of
interest under ODbL 1.0, population under CC BY 4.0. The Leuven case uses
Telraam data under CC BY-NC 4.0 and is for non-commercial use only.
